coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

coursesExamined.contribution: MandatoryYear1personal/academicdevelopment.

coursesExamined.name: Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
evidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct method: research design, sampling, experimental/survey techniques and descriptive/inferential statistics support developmental and educational inquiry; a general group project is not a teaching placement.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Data Science

evidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
evidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
evidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
evidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary method: data cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and an independent data-analysis project supply concrete skills for empirical developmental and educational questions; the datasets are not necessarily educational.

coursesExamined.name: Ethics

evidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
evidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary normative study: moral theories, responsibility and equality support critical decisions involving children and educational practice; no dedicated Dutch child/education-law syllabus is claimed.

coursesExamined.name: Philosophy of Mind

evidence.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
evidence.topics: Persons and personal identity; Psychological and narrative theories of identity; Buddhist non-self; Split-brain cases and self-knowledge; Behaviourism; Physicalism and functionalism; Mind-body problem; Content externalism and internalism; AI intelligence and consciousness; Virtual reality; Dreaming and perception; Transformative experience; Value of conscious experience; Animal minds
evidence.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual analysis; Reconstruction and evaluation of arguments; Comparison of theories of mind; Literature-based philosophical research
evidence.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary conceptual foundation: theories of mind, behaviourism, physicalism, identity and neuropsychological cases examine assumptions behind accounts of cognition and developing persons. It does not teach child-development stages or philosophy of science as a dedicated sequence.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Sociology

evidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
evidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
evidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation
evidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary social analysis: institutions, social interaction, inequality, race, gender and class support interpretation of the social environments in which upbringing and learning occur; not sociology of education as a dedicated syllabus.

coursesExamined.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

evidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
evidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
evidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
evidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct research method: qualitative design, collection, interpretation, reflexivity and group inquiry support the study of educational relationships and practice; topics are not guaranteed to be educational.

coursesExamined.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

evidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
evidence.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
evidence.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design
evidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary social foundation: trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity and research on civil-society organisations explain the collective environments in which upbringing and education occur. No school-specific research assignment is guaranteed.

coursesExamined.name: Perception & Action

evidence.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct cognitive mechanisms: sensory processing and goal-directed action inform understanding of perceptual/motor functioning; not the comparator’s dedicated child motor-development course.

coursesExamined.name: Higher Order Functions

evidence.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
evidence.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
evidence.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review
evidence.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct cognition: memory, emotion, attention, social cognition and experimental reasoning address mechanisms underlying learning and development; the syllabus is not specifically developmental neuropsychology.

coursesExamined.name: Psycholinguistics

evidence.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct cognition/language: acquisition, reading/dyslexia, bilingualism, comprehension and language impairments respond to the target’s cognitive/language and learning questions; not language-teaching didactics.

coursesExamined.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine

evidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
evidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
evidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments
evidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary biological foundation: cells, inheritance, physiology and cellular communication ground the programme’s study of biological influences on development and prepare for adult physiology; this is not child pedagogy.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior

evidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
evidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
evidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis
evidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct foundations: nature–nurture, mental processes, brain function and psychological/neuroscientific methods ground study of typical and atypical development.

coursesExamined.name: Human Physiology

evidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
evidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
evidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision
evidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary physiological foundation: adult organ systems, homeostasis, integration, metabolism, growth and ageing support understanding of biological functioning and bodily influences on development; not a paediatric or child motor-development course.

coursesExamined.name: Social Psychology

evidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
evidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
evidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study
evidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct psychological foundations: theories of social influence on thoughts, feelings and behaviour support analysis of relationships and social development; the course is not child-specific.

coursesExamined.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods

evidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
evidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
evidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
evidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct quantitative method: regression, factor analysis, covariance models and logistic/nonparametric analyses support behavioural evidence and measurement questions; not a complete psychometrics and decision-science course.

coursesExamined.name: Psychopathology

evidence.profile: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
evidence.topics: Mental-disorder concepts and stigma; Historical and contemporary psychopathology; Biopsychosocial causation; Clinical assessment and diagnostic classification; Stress and health; Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders; Mood disorders; Somatic and dissociative disorders; Psychotic disorders; Eating and personality disorders; Substance-related and neurocognitive disorders; Sexuality and mental health; Childhood and adolescent disorders; Forensic psychology; Culture and emotion regulation
evidence.methods: Diagnostic case analysis; Application and critique of DSM criteria; Biopsychosocial case formulation; Structured literature searching and screening; Source-quality appraisal; Evidence synthesis; Critical evaluation of etiological and intervention models
evidence.description2: The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills, explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct psychopathology: a lifespan biopsychosocial study of disorders, assessment and treatment perspectives supports atypical-development inquiry; it is not specialist child or orthopedagogical training.

coursesExamined.name: Medical & Health Psychology

evidence.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
evidence.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
evidence.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis
evidence.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary health psychology: biopsychosocial explanations of stress, health behaviour and chronic illness support analysis of wellbeing and vulnerability across the lifespan, including their consequences for development.

coursesExamined.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies

evidence.profile: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
evidence.topics: Clinical attitude and ethics; Diagnostic classification; Reliability and validity; Clinical interviews; Personality inventories and projective techniques; Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment; Behavioural and biological assessment; Psychological reporting; Psychodynamic and behavioural therapies; Cognitive therapy and CBT; Person-centered and family therapies; Integrative psychotherapy; Treatment outcomes and evidence; Child and adolescent clinical psychology
evidence.methods: Clinical interviewing practice; Introductory psychological-test administration, scoring and interpretation; Psychometric appraisal; Behavioural observation; Integration of assessment data; Psychodiagnostic report writing; Clinical case and therapy-session analysis; Reflective monitoring of clinical skills
evidence.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct clinical perspective: psychological assessment and psychotherapies across age groups, including children, provide evidence and ethical frameworks for developmental-support questions; no practitioner competence or orthopedagogy qualification is implied.

coursesExamined.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
evidence.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
evidence.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting
evidence.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct research method: systematic reviews, meta-analysis, effect sizes and R support evidence-based developmental/educational judgments; it synthesises existing studies and does not supply the comparator’s separate primary-research thesis.

coursesExamined.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology

evidence.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
evidence.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
evidence.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports
evidence.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct developmental core: physical, cognitive, social and emotional development from prenatal life through adulthood, including childhood and adolescence, substantially responds to the target’s defining developmental questions.

coursesExamined.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism

evidence.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.
evidence.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
evidence.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools
evidence.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct, bounded educational application: research and evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators address democratic school culture, supportive learning environments, empathy and mental wellbeing; not a general special-needs curriculum.

coursesExamined.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication

evidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design
evidence.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

coursesExamined.contribution: Complementary academic skill: argument structure, academic essays and oral presentation support research communication and provide preparation for designing primary-school speaking activities.

coursesExamined.name: Rhetoric in Action

evidence.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
evidence.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
evidence.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation
evidence.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

coursesExamined.contribution: Direct, bounded educational application: students design and teach speaking/debating exercises to primary-school pupils in a community-engaged course; it is not a full Pabo placement or general didactics sequence.
